name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWS_OF_MOTION_SEQUENCING_Q01 - Logical sequence of problem solving in mechanics

questiontext.text:
Consider the following steps recommended for systematically analyzing and solving problems in mechanics using free-body diagrams:

  1. Choose a convenient part of the assembly of bodies as the system.
  2. Draw a schematic diagram showing the various parts of the assembly, links, and supports.
  3. Draw a free-body diagram showing the chosen system and all the external forces acting on it.
  4. Apply Newton's laws of motion to formulate equations and solve for the unknown forces or accelerations.
  5. Identify and mark the known forces (magnitudes and directions) and treat the remaining forces as unknowns.

Choose the correct logical sequence of these steps from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understanding the systematic methodology in mechanics
According to standard mechanical analysis (as detailed in Section 4.11 of the NCERT physics curriculum), solving an assembly of interacting bodies requires a structured, step-by-step procedure to avoid omitting forces or misapplying Newton's laws.

Step 2: Logical ordering of the steps
The procedure develops sequentially as follows:

  • First, one must construct a schematic overview of the entire physical assembly, including all interacting bodies, supports, strings, and pulleys (Step II).
  • Next, from this overall assembly, one isolates a specific, convenient body or group of bodies to define the chosen system (Step I).
  • Once the system boundary is chosen, a separate free-body diagram of this isolated system is drawn, explicitly displaying all external forces acting upon it due to the environment and other bodies (Step III).
  • On this free-body diagram, one then indicates all given or known forces (such as gravity, applied forces, and string directions) while labeling the remaining forces as unknown quantities to be determined (Step V).
  • Finally, using Newton's second and third laws of motion along appropriate coordinate axes, one writes the equations of motion and solves for the unknown quantities (Step IV).

Step 3: Final Answer
The correct logical sequence is II → I → III → V → IV.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWS_OF_MOTION_SEQUENCING_Q02 - Chronological sequence of Galileos law of inertia discovery

questiontext.text:
The following observations and deductions represent key stages in Galileo's investigation that led to the discovery of the law of inertia:

  1. Observing that a ball released on one inclined plane rolls down and climbs up an opposite inclined plane to almost the same height.
  2. Observing that an object moving down an inclined plane accelerates, while an object moving up an inclined plane retards.
  3. Deducing that in the limiting case where the slope of the second plane is reduced to zero (a horizontal plane), the ball must travel an infinite distance at constant velocity in the absence of friction.
  4. Deducing that motion on a frictionless horizontal plane is an intermediate state characterized by neither acceleration nor retardation (constant velocity).
  5. Observing that when the slope of the second opposing plane is decreased, the ball still reaches the same height, thereby traveling a longer distance.

Choose the correct chronological and logical sequence of these stages:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Historical and Conceptual Context
Galileo overturned the Aristotelian fallacy through a series of systematic observations on inclined planes, generalizing from real rolling motion to idealized frictionless motion.

Step 2: Chronological and Logical Development
The logical progression of Galileo's insight unfolds as follows:

  • He began by observing single inclined planes: bodies rolling downward accelerate under gravity, whereas bodies rolling upward decelerate (retard) (Step II).
  • From these two opposing behaviors, he reasoned that motion on a horizontal plane represents an intermediate condition where there is neither downward acceleration nor upward retardation, implying uniform velocity if friction were negligible (Step IV).
  • To test this hypothesis rigorously, he devised the double inclined plane experiment, observing that a ball rolling down one plane climbs the opposite plane to reach virtually the same initial height (Step I).
  • He then reduced the inclination (slope) of the second plane and observed that the ball continued to climb to the same vertical height, traversing a progressively greater path length (Step V).
  • Extrapolating this to the limiting case where the slope of the second plane becomes zero (a flat horizontal plane), he concluded that the ball would never reach its original height and therefore must continue moving indefinitely with constant velocity in the absence of friction (Step III).

Step 3: Final Answer
The correct sequence is II → IV → I → V → III.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWS_OF_MOTION_SEQUENCING_Q03 - Progressive sequence of frictional regimes under applied force

questiontext.text:
A heavy wooden box is initially at rest on a rough horizontal floor. A horizontal pushing force is applied to the box and is continuously increased from zero until the box slides across the floor with constant speed. Consider the following stages of frictional response:

  1. Kinetic friction of constant magnitude \( f_k = \mu_k N \) acts opposite to the sliding velocity.
  2. Frictional force is zero since no external force acts along the horizontal contact surface.
  3. The frictional force reaches its maximum possible static threshold value, \( f_{s,\max} = \mu_s N \).
  4. As the applied force increases, the static friction increases equally and opposite to the applied force, keeping the box at rest.
  5. Relative sliding begins and the frictional force abruptly drops slightly below the peak static value.

Choose the correct sequence of stages in chronological order as the applied force increases:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principles of Friction
Frictional resistance between two solid surfaces in contact exhibits distinct physical regimes: static friction (self-adjusting up to a limiting threshold), transition to motion, and kinetic friction.

Step 2: Sequential Analysis as Applied Force Increases
Tracing the state of friction from zero force to sliding:

  • Initially, before any external horizontal force is applied, static friction does not exist independently; hence the frictional force is zero (Step II).
  • When a small horizontal force is applied, static friction comes into play. It is a self-adjusting contact force that matches the applied force in magnitude and opposes it in direction, keeping the box stationary with zero net acceleration (Step IV).
  • As the pushing force is continuously increased, the static friction increases until it reaches the maximum limit that the contact surfaces can sustain, which is the limiting friction \( f_{s,\max} = \mu_s N \) (Step III).
  • When the applied force slightly exceeds this limiting threshold, the box breaks free from interlocking surface asperities and starts sliding; during this initiation of relative motion, the frictional resistance decreases slightly (Step V).
  • Once sustained sliding motion is established, the opposing force is kinetic friction \( f_k = \mu_k N \), which remains nearly constant and independent of sliding speed over a broad range (Step I).

Step 3: Final Answer
The correct chronological sequence is II → IV → III → V → I.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWS_OF_MOTION_SEQUENCING_Q04 - Chronological stages of momentum transfer during collision

questiontext.text:
Two isolated interacting particles, A and B, undergo a direct collision in space free from external forces. Arrange the following events and physical processes in the correct chronological order from start to finish:

  1. Particles A and B make contact, and large mutual interaction forces \( \mathbf{F}_{AB} \) and \( \mathbf{F}_{BA} \) act simultaneously on each other over a very brief collision duration \( \Delta t \).
  2. Particles A and B approach each other with constant initial velocities and initial linear momenta \( \mathbf{p}_A \) and \( \mathbf{p}_B \).
  3. Particles A and B separate and move independently with constant final linear momenta \( \mathbf{p}'_A \) and \( \mathbf{p}'_B \), such that \( \mathbf{p}'_A + \mathbf{p}'_B = \mathbf{p}_A + \mathbf{p}_B \).
  4. The mutual impulsive forces cause momentum changes \( \Delta \mathbf{p}_A = \mathbf{F}_{AB} \Delta t \) and \( \Delta \mathbf{p}_B = \mathbf{F}_{BA} \Delta t \) for the individual particles.
  5. By Newton's third law, \( \mathbf{F}_{AB} = -\mathbf{F}_{BA} \) at every instant, ensuring that the net impulse on the combined two-particle system vanishes (\( \Delta \mathbf{p}_A + \Delta \mathbf{p}_B = 0 \)).

Choose the correct sequence of events from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying the System and Applicable Laws
The problem describes an isolated two-body collision governed by Newton's second law (impulse equals momentum change), Newton's third law (simultaneous equal and opposite action-reaction forces), and the resulting conservation of linear momentum.

Step 2: Logical and Chronological Ordering
The interaction progresses in the following order:

  • Prior to contact, the particles travel freely through space with constant velocities and initial momenta \( \mathbf{p}_A \) and \( \mathbf{p}_B \) because the net external force is zero (Step II).
  • The collision begins when the surfaces come into contact, exerting large mutual contact forces \( \mathbf{F}_{AB} \) and \( \mathbf{F}_{BA} \) over a short interaction time interval \( \Delta t \) (Step I).
  • During this interaction, each particle experiences an impulse that alters its individual momentum according to Newton's second law: \( \Delta \mathbf{p}_A = \mathbf{F}_{AB} \Delta t \) and \( \Delta \mathbf{p}_B = \mathbf{F}_{BA} \Delta t \) (Step IV).
  • Because action and reaction forces are strictly equal and opposite at every instant (\( \mathbf{F}_{AB} = -\mathbf{F}_{BA} \)), the sum of the two impulses cancels out completely: \( \mathbf{F}_{AB} \Delta t + \mathbf{F}_{BA} \Delta t = 0 \implies \Delta \mathbf{p}_A + \Delta \mathbf{p}_B = 0 \) (Step V).
  • Finally, the bodies separate and move apart with final momenta \( \mathbf{p}'_A \) and \( \mathbf{p}'_B \), with total system momentum conserved: \( \mathbf{p}'_A + \mathbf{p}'_B = \mathbf{p}_A + \mathbf{p}_B \) (Step III).

Step 3: Final Answer
The correct sequence is II → I → IV → V → III.
